stem: Which security makes its holder a creditor rather than an owner of the company?

options.rationale: Correct: a debenture is a loan to the company.
Ordinary shareholders are owners.
Preference shareholders are also owners.
This is still a share, so its holder is an owner.

explanation: Debenture holders lend to the company; shareholders own it.

stem: Which shareholders normally have voting rights at the annual general meeting?

options.rationale: Correct: one vote per ordinary share.
They usually have no vote.
They are lenders, not shareholders.
Suppliers are not members of the company.

explanation: Ordinary shareholders control the company through their votes.

stem: A company makes a loss this year. Which payment must it still make?

options.rationale: Dividends are paid only from profits.
Preference dividends also need profits.
Bonuses are not compulsory.
Correct: interest on a loan is due whether or not there is a profit.

explanation: Debenture interest is a fixed charge on the company.

stem: What is special about a cumulative preference share?

options.rationale: Its rate is fixed.

options.content: Unpaid dividends are carried forward and paid later
options.rationale: Correct: arrears are paid before ordinary dividends.

options.content: It gives the holder extra votes
options.rationale: Preference shares usually carry no vote.

options.content: It can never be bought back by the company
options.rationale: That depends on whether it is redeemable.

explanation: Cumulative preference shareholders do not lose a missed dividend.

stem: What is authorised capital?

options.content: The capital shareholders have actually paid
options.rationale: That is paid-up capital.

options.content: The capital the company has asked for so far
options.rationale: That is called-up capital.

options.content: The maximum share capital a company may issue
options.rationale: Correct: stated in its founding documents.
Debentures are loan capital, not share capital.

explanation: Authorised ≥ issued ≥ called-up ≥ paid-up.

stem: An investor wants a steady, fixed return and is prepared to give up voting rights. Which security suits her best?

options.rationale: Dividends vary and holders have votes.
Correct: fixed dividend paid before ordinary shares; usually no vote.
Not a company security.
Stagging is short-term speculation.

explanation: Preference shares give a fixed dividend with priority over ordinary shares.
hints: Which share has a fixed rate but no vote?

stem: Why might the existing shareholders prefer the company to issue debentures rather than new ordinary shares?

options.content: Debenture interest is never paid in loss years
options.rationale: It must be paid in loss years.

options.content: Debentures never have to be repaid
options.rationale: Debentures are repaid at the end of the term.

options.content: Debenture holders share in all future profits
options.rationale: They receive only fixed interest.

options.content: Their control of the company is not diluted
options.rationale: Correct: debenture holders have no votes.

explanation: Debt finance keeps voting control with existing shareholders.

stem: A company is wound up. In what order are these groups repaid?

options.rationale: This is the reverse order.

options.content: Preference shareholders, debenture holders, then ordinary
options.rationale: Debenture holders, as creditors, come before shareholders.

options.content: Debenture holders, preference, then ordinary shareholders
options.rationale: Correct: creditors first, ordinary shareholders last.

options.content: All three groups are repaid at the same time
options.rationale: There is a strict order of priority.

explanation: Creditors (including debenture holders) are repaid before shareholders; preference before ordinary.

stem: A company has 120,000 ordinary shares of US\$1 each and 40,000 7% preference shares of US\$1 each. Profit available for dividends is US\$21,400. Calculate the ordinary dividend as a percentage of the nominal value, to one decimal place.
explanation: Preference dividend = 7% × 40,000 = US\$2,800; left for ordinary = US\$18,600; per share = US\$0.1550; = 15.5%.
workedSolution:
1. Preference dividend = 7% × 40,000 = 2,800.
2. Left for ordinary shareholders = 21,400 − 2,800 = 18,600.
3. Ordinary dividend % = 18,600 ÷ 120,000 × 100 = 15.5%.
hints: Divide what is left by the ordinary share capital.

stem: A company has issued US\$65,000 of 9% debentures. How much interest must it pay each year?
A company has issued shares worth US\$150,000. It has called up US\$120,000, and shareholders have paid US\$112,500. What are the calls in arrear?
explanation: Calls in arrear = called-up − paid-up = 120,000 − 112,500 = US\$7,500.
workedSolution: 1. Calls in arrear = called-up − paid-up = 120,000 − 112,500 = US\$7,500.
hints: Calls in arrear are amounts asked for but not yet paid.

stem: Preference dividends are paid before ordinary dividends.
explanation: True. That is the "preference" they enjoy.

stem: Paid-up capital can be greater than called-up capital.
explanation: False. Shareholders cannot have paid more than has been called: authorised ≥ issued ≥ called-up ≥ paid-up.

stem: What is the name for the part of a company's profit paid to its shareholders?
explanation: A dividend.

stem: Distinguish between shares and debentures (two differences).

points.description: Shareholders are owners; debenture holders are lenders/creditors (1)
Dividends vary and need profit; debenture interest is fixed and paid even in a loss / votes versus no votes / repayment order (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Shareholders own the company, whereas debenture holders have lent it money and are creditors. Shareholders receive dividends only when there are profits, while debenture holders receive fixed interest every year, even when the company makes a loss.

explanation: Each difference must contrast both securities.
hints: What happens in a loss year?

stem: Explain why ordinary shares are said to carry the greatest risk.

points.description: Dividends vary and may be nil in a bad year (1)
Paid only after debenture interest and preference dividends (1)
Repaid last if the company is wound up / may receive nothing (1)
In return they may earn the highest dividends and control the company (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Ordinary shareholders receive dividends only after debenture interest and preference dividends have been paid, so in a poor year they may get nothing. If the company is wound up, they are repaid last and may lose their capital. In return, they control the company and can earn high dividends in good years.

explanation: Ordinary shareholders come last for income and capital.
hints: Where do they stand in the order of payment?
